title: Participles: active forms

objectives.can: Parse present and aorist active participles: tense, case, number and gender.

explanation.summary: A participle is a verb that behaves like an adjective. It has a tense stem and a voice like any verb, and it has case, number and gender like any adjective. This lesson teaches the active forms of the present, the aorist and the perfect.

sections.heading: A verb that agrees like an adjective
body: A finite verb has person, number, tense, voice and mood. A participle has no person and no mood. Instead it has case, number and gender, and it takes them from the word it goes with. In Mark 1:7 λέγων is nominative singular masculine because it describes the subject of the clause, the one who was proclaiming. In Mark 5:27 ἀκούσασα is nominative singular feminine because the woman in the story is the one who heard.

So parsing a participle has two halves. The stem and the ending of the verb part tell you the tense and the voice. The adjective endings tell you the case, number and gender. To find out what the participle is doing in its sentence you also need the word it agrees with, and that is the subject of Stage 5. This lesson is only about the forms.

sections.heading: The present active participle
body: Take the present stem and add -ων, -ουσα, -ον for the nominative singular masculine, feminine and neuter. λέγων, λέγουσα, λέγον are the forms of λέγω. The masculine and neuter belong to the third declension, with the stem -οντ- showing in the genitive: -οντος. The feminine is a first-declension noun with the ending -ουσα, genitive -ουσης, and every case of it follows the pattern of a first-declension noun.

The dative plural of the masculine and neuter is -ουσι(ν), because the -ντ- falls out before -σι. That is why λέγουσιν can be a present active participle in the dative plural as well as a finite verb, 'they say'. Only the context tells you which.

sections.heading: The aorist active participle
body: The first aorist participle puts -σα- between the stem and the endings: -σας, -σασα, -σαν, with -σαντ- as the stem of the masculine and neuter. ἀκούσας is nominative singular masculine and ἀκούσασα is nominative singular feminine. Verbs whose stems end in λ, μ, ν or ρ have no σ and use -ας, -ασα, -αν. There is no augment in the participle: the augment belongs to the indicative.

The second aorist participle looks like the present, with the endings -ων, -ουσα, -ον, but it is built on the aorist stem. It is recognised by the stem and by the accent. Compare the present λέγων, with the accent on the stem, to λαβών and ἐλθών, with the accent on the ending. In the feminine too the accent falls on the ending: λαβοῦσα, ἐλθοῦσα. Where the stem is the same as the present, as in εἰπών, you rely on the accent and on what you know of the verb.

sections.heading: The perfect active participle
body: The perfect participle keeps the reduplication of the perfect stem and adds -κ- in most verbs, then the endings -κώς, -κυῖα, -κός. The genitive is -κότος in the masculine and neuter and -κυίας in the feminine. So πεπιστευκότας in John 8:31 is accusative plural masculine, and ἐληλυθυῖαν is accusative singular feminine. Not every verb has the -κ-: the perfect of some verbs is formed without it, but the endings stay the same.

The perfect participle is much rarer than the present and the aorist. Learn to spot it by the reduplication at the front and the endings -ως, -υια, -ος at the back. A future active participle also exists (-σων, -σουσα, -σον). It is rare, and it is formed like the present participle on the future stem.

sections.heading: A routine for parsing
body: First look for the signs of the tense: -ντ- or -ουσ- on the present stem, -σαντ- or -σασ- for the first aorist, reduplication and -κ- for the perfect. Then look at the ending for the case, number and gender, using what you know of the article and the third declension. Then check against the word the participle describes: it must agree with it in all three. If it does not, you have misparsed, or the participle stands by itself as a noun.

misunderstandings: Taking every -ων for a participle. The same ending is the genitive plural of many nouns, such as λόγων. A participle also has a stem and a meaning of its own as a verb, and it agrees with something.

Taking every -σας for a second person singular. The second person singular of the first aorist indicative has the same ending, but it also has an augment and the participle has none. The accusative plural of many first-declension nouns also ends in -ας.
Reading the tense as time. In the participle the present and the aorist mainly show how the action is viewed, not when it happened. The next lessons say more.

Forgetting the feminine. The feminine participle is not third declension: it declines like a first-declension noun and has the stem in -ουσ- or -σασ-, which is why the genitive is -ουσης and not -οντος.

deeper.heading: Why the nominative singular looks different
body: The nominative singular masculine is formed from the stem plus -ς. In the present, the stem λεγοντ- plus -ς loses the -ντ-, and the vowel before it is lengthened to -ων. In the first aorist the stem -σαντ- loses the -ντ- in the same way, and the result is -σας. In the dative plural the same loss happens before -σι.

In the other cases the -ντ- stays in the masculine and neuter (-οντος, -οντα), and for that reason the forms with -ντ- are the best sign of a participle that you can find in the genitive and accusative.
